topic: Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: Which statement about background radiation is correct?
items.correct: It is around us all of the time, from natural and from man-made sources.
items.misconception: It is present only in an area that a nuclear accident has affected.
items.why: Radiation is reported in the news almost only in connection with accidents and weapons, so students tie its presence to disaster rather than to ordinary life. Background radiation is present continuously and everywhere. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space as well as from man-made sources. An accident raises the level in a place; it does not create radiation where there was none.
items.random_wrong: It exists only because people have built reactors and weapons.

items.q: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?
items.correct: Cosmic rays that reach the Earth's surface from space
items.misconception: Fallout still present from earlier nuclear weapons tests
items.why: Students classify a source by what the material is made of rather than by how it came to be there, and once fallout has settled into soil it looks like part of the ground. Sources are classified by origin. Fallout is in the environment because people tested weapons or because a reactor failed, so it is man-made, however ordinary the atoms in it may be.
items.random_wrong: Radioactive waste kept in a store at a power plant

items.q: An accident at a nuclear power station releases radioactive material that settles over nearby farmland. How should this contribution to the background radiation there be classified?
items.correct: As man-made, because human activity released it
items.misconception: As natural, because the isotopes also occur in rocks
items.why: Students classify a source by what the material is made of rather than by how it came to be there, and once fallout has settled into soil it looks like part of the ground. Sources are classified by origin. Fallout is in the environment because people tested weapons or because a reactor failed, so it is man-made, however ordinary the atoms in it may be.
items.random_wrong: As natural, since the fallout now lies in soil

items.q: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?
items.correct: Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents
items.misconception: Cosmic rays from space and rocks lying in the earth
items.why: The man-made sources are the ones with memorable names and stories attached, so they dominate a student's picture of where radiation comes from. Rocks and cosmic rays from space are natural sources and have always contributed. Man-made sources such as fallout add to this natural background; they are not the whole of it.
items.random_wrong: Rocks in the ground and waste from nuclear accidents

items.q: A radiographer in a hospital records a higher annual radiation dose than an office worker who lives in the same street. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: Her occupation exposes her to radiation that the office worker never meets.
items.misconception: Everyone receives the same dose, so the readings must be faulty.
items.why: The word background suggests a constant baseline, and textbook figures are often quoted as a single average value with no range given. The level varies. Living where the rock is granite, or at high altitude, raises the dose from natural sources, and some occupations bring extra exposure on top of that.
items.random_wrong: Radiation collects in the body of anybody who works indoors all day.

items.q: People living where the local rock is granite, and aircrew who fly long-haul routes, both receive above-average annual radiation doses. Which statement explains both cases?
items.correct: Location affects dose: granite gives radon, altitude gives cosmic rays.
items.misconception: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests gathers on high ground and on granite.
items.why: Students classify a source by what the material is made of rather than by how it came to be there, and once fallout has settled into soil it looks like part of the ground. Sources are classified by origin. Fallout is in the environment because people tested weapons or because a reactor failed, so it is man-made, however ordinary the atoms in it may be.
items.random_wrong: Both groups spend much more of their working time above sea level.

items.q: A safety leaflet states that a worker received a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv during one year. What does this dose value describe?
items.correct: The risk of harm to her body from the radiation absorbed.
items.misconception: The number of counts that her detector recorded each second.
items.why: Both units appear in the same topic and both get larger when there is more radiation, so students merge them into one idea. Activity counts decays per second in a source. Dose measures the harm risked by a body that absorbs radiation, and two people beside the same source can receive very different doses.
items.random_wrong: The number of nuclei that decayed in the sources she used.

items.q: A patient's total radiation dose over a course of treatment is 2500 mSv. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?
items.correct: 2.5 Sv
items.why: Students learn conversions as 'find the number and multiply' without deciding first whether the answer should come out larger or smaller than the value they started with. Check the size of the answer. A millisievert is smaller than a sievert, so a dose in mSv must give a smaller number when written in Sv: divide by 1000.

items.q: A worker's badge records a dose of 45 mSv over one year. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?
items.misconception: 45 Sv
items.why: Students learn conversions as 'find the number and multiply' without deciding first whether the answer should come out larger or smaller than the value they started with. Check the size of the answer. A millisievert is smaller than a sievert, so a dose in mSv must give a smaller number when written in Sv: divide by 1000.

items.q: Which statement about the half-life values of radioactive isotopes is correct?
items.correct: They cover a very wide range, from fractions of a second to billions of years.
items.misconception: They are all much the same, since every unstable nucleus decays at a similar rate.
items.why: Practice questions use convenient half-lives of minutes, days or years so that graphs fit on a page, so the extremes are never seen. The range is enormous, from small fractions of a second to thousands of millions of years, and that range is what makes some isotopes suitable as tracers and others a long-term waste problem.
items.random_wrong: They all lie between a few seconds and a few days, for any isotope at all.

items.q: A radioactive isotope with a half-life of many thousands of years is spilled onto open ground. Why is such a long half-life a particular hazard here?
items.correct: The ground stays radioactive for a very long time after the spill.
items.misconception: Its activity is enormous, so it emits a great deal of radiation now.
items.why: Long is read as more, and the long-lived isotopes in nuclear waste are the ones talked about as dangerous, so the two ideas fuse. For a given number of atoms, a long half-life means decays are rare, so the activity is low. The danger is duration: the material remains a hazard long after it has been spilled or buried.
items.random_wrong: Isotopes with a long half-life always emit alpha, the worst kind of all.

items.q: A source with a half-life of a few minutes is spilled in a school laboratory. Why is it a serious hazard at once but much less of one an hour later?
items.correct: Its activity is high at first and then falls away fast.
items.misconception: The nuclei all stop decaying once one half-life has gone by.
items.why: Students learn that short-lived tracers are chosen to protect patients and conclude that short half-life is simply a synonym for safe. A short half-life means many decays each second at the beginning, so the immediate hazard is large. It becomes safe later, not now, and that is exactly why it must be handled carefully at first.
items.random_wrong: A short half-life means it gives out no radiation at all.

items.q: A tracer is injected so that a doctor can watch how a patient's kidneys are working. Which property makes an isotope suitable for this use?
items.correct: It emits gamma radiation, which leaves the body and is detected outside.
items.misconception: It emits alpha radiation, which is easily detected through the skin.
items.why: Students associate strong ionisation with a strong signal, and they do not check whether the radiation can escape the body to reach a detector at all. Alpha is absorbed within a few centimetres of tissue, so nothing reaches the detector and all of the ionisation is deposited in the patient. Gamma is weakly ionising and penetrating, which is what a tracer needs.
items.random_wrong: It has a half-life of many years, so the scan could be repeated later.

items.q: How are nuclear radiations used to control or destroy a tumour lying deep inside the body?
items.correct: A high dose of gamma radiation is aimed at the tumour from outside.
items.misconception: A weak alpha source is swallowed and travels to the tumour site itself.
items.why: Students associate strong ionisation with a strong signal, and they do not check whether the radiation can escape the body to reach a detector at all. Alpha is absorbed within a few centimetres of tissue, so nothing reaches the detector and all of the ionisation is deposited in the patient. Gamma is weakly ionising and penetrating, which is what a tracer needs.
items.random_wrong: A tracer is injected and its gamma rays then shrink the tumour.

items.q: A gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of about six hours is chosen instead of one with a half-life of several years. Evaluate this choice.
items.correct: Good: the activity falls quickly, so the patient's dose after the scan stays small.
items.misconception: Poor: a source that decays this quickly cannot give out enough radiation to be detected.
items.why: Students learn that short-lived tracers are chosen to protect patients and conclude that short half-life is simply a synonym for safe. A short half-life means many decays each second at the beginning, so the immediate hazard is large. It becomes safe later, not now, and that is exactly why it must be handled carefully at first.
items.random_wrong: It makes no difference: the tracer leaves the body within a day whatever its half-life.

items.q: A scan using a radioactive tracer gives a patient a dose of about 6 mSv. The average annual dose from background radiation is about 2.7 mSv. The patient refuses the scan, saying that any nuclear radiation is too dangerous. Which is the best evaluation of that decision?
items.correct: The small added risk should be weighed against the benefit of a diagnosis.
items.misconception: The dose is close to one year of background radiation, so there is no risk.
items.why: Radiation is presented in public discussion as uniquely dangerous, and students have no everyday scale on which to judge one dose figure against another. Risk is a matter of degree. A dose of a few millisieverts raises the chance of harm only slightly, while an undiagnosed or untreated illness may be far more dangerous, so given data must be compared, not simply rejected.
items.random_wrong: Refusing is right, because man-made radiation harms the body more than background.

items.q: Are cosmic rays simply a part of ordinary sunlight?
items.correct: No. Cosmic rays are ionising radiation arriving from space, and they reach us by night as well as by day.
items.misconception: Cosmic rays are just sunlight, so you only receive them outdoors on a sunny day.
items.why: The only radiation from space that students meet daily is sunlight, so 'from space' is read as 'from the Sun', and the word rays reinforces it. Cosmic rays are high-energy ionising radiation from space that reaches the Earth all of the time. The atmosphere absorbs much of it, which is why the dose is larger at high altitude.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Aircrew are far above the rocks in the ground. Does that mean they receive a smaller dose?
items.correct: No. At altitude there is less atmosphere above you to absorb cosmic rays, so the dose is larger.
items.misconception: Height puts you further from the radioactive rocks, so background radiation must fall as you go up.
items.why: Students remember one natural source, the ground, and reason only about distance from it, forgetting that cosmic rays arrive from the other direction. Two natural sources act in opposite directions with height. The contribution from rock falls, but the cosmic ray contribution rises much more because less air shields you, so the total dose goes up.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a radiation dose in sieverts tell you how much radioactive material a person contains?
items.correct: No. Dose is a measure of the risk of harm to the body from the radiation it has absorbed.
items.misconception: A dose is like a dose of medicine: it is the quantity of radioactive substance given to the patient.
items.why: In every other context a dose is an amount of a substance, so students carry that meaning across without questioning it. Radiation dose measures the effect on the body, not an amount of material. It depends on how much radiation was absorbed and on the type of radiation, and it is measured in sieverts.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In radiotherapy, is healthy tissue completely unaffected because the beam is aimed at the tumour?
items.correct: No. Tissue in the path of the beam also receives a dose, which is why the treatment has side effects.
items.misconception: Targeting means that only the tumour receives radiation, so radiotherapy carries no risk to the rest of the body.
items.why: The word targeted, and diagrams showing a single arrow striking a tumour, suggest that the radiation begins and ends at the target. The beam must pass through healthy tissue to reach a tumour inside the body. Rotating the beam around the patient keeps the tumour in the path while spreading the dose to healthy tissue over a larger volume.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a patient given a radioactive tracer stay radioactive permanently?
items.correct: No. The activity falls as the isotope decays, and a short half-life is chosen so that it falls quickly.
items.misconception: Once a radioactive substance is inside you, you remain radioactive for the rest of your life.
items.why: Students think of the substance as contamination that cannot be removed, and they do not connect that idea to the decay curve they have drawn in another lesson. The nuclei decay, so the activity falls. A tracer with a half-life of a few hours has almost no activity left after a day, and it is also gradually excreted from the body.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
